scenarios.b: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.

You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.

bank.q: An engineer's loop terminates when the assistant's text contains the word "resolved," or after a hard cap of 5 iterations. In production the agent sometimes stops mid-task and sometimes loops past a finished task. What is the correct loop-control mechanism?
o: Raise the iteration cap from 5 to 20 to give the agent more room to finish
Continue while `stop_reason` is "tool_use" and terminate when it is "end_turn", appending each tool result to the conversation history between iterations
Parse the assistant's natural-language output for completion phrases like "resolved" or "done"
Terminate the loop as soon as any tool call returns successfully
bank.w: Loop control keys on `stop_reason` (continue on "tool_use", stop on "end_turn"), appending tool results each iteration.  A (arbitrary cap), C (parsing natural-language signals), and D (first-success) are the three anti-patterns the guide names — they stop early or loop forever.

bank.q: A coordinator's loop terminates after a hard cap of 3 model turns. For complex topics it stops before the report subagent runs, producing truncated reports. What is the correct primary stopping mechanism?
o: Raise the cap to a fixed 10 turns for every query
Stop once the assistant's text output contains the phrase "final report"
Stop as soon as the synthesize subagent returns any output
Terminate when `stop_reason` is "end_turn"; keep a generous turn cap only as a safety backstop, not the primary control
bank.w: Termination is driven by `stop_reason == "end_turn"`; a turn cap belongs only as a safety backstop.  A is still an arbitrary cap; B parses assistant text (anti-pattern); C stops before the report stage.

bank.q: Two search subagents researching "renewable energy policy" return heavily overlapping sources, wasting effort. The coordinator gave both the same broad prompt. What best addresses this?
o: Partition the research scope across subagents — assign each a distinct subtopic or source type — to minimize duplication
Have the synthesize subagent deduplicate the overlapping sources afterward
Reduce to a single search subagent and accept slower research
Run the two subagents sequentially so the second can avoid the first's sources
bank.w: Partitioning scope (distinct subtopics/source types) prevents duplication at the source.  B dedupes downstream after the effort is wasted; C loses parallelism; D serial work is slower and still guesses at overlap.

bank.q: After synthesis, the coordinator detects that the draft report has no coverage of one required subtopic. What orchestration pattern best resolves this?
o: Ship the report with an explicit note that the subtopic is missing
Restart the entire pipeline from the original query

An iterative refinement loop: the coordinator evaluates synthesis output for gaps, re-delegates targeted queries to the search/analysis subagents, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient
Have the report subagent fill the gap from its own general knowledge
bank.w: An iterative refinement loop — detect gaps, re-delegate targeted queries, re-synthesize — is the designed fix.  A ships a known gap; B wastes completed work; D fabricates unattributed content.

bank.q: Telemetry shows 70% of incoming queries are simple single-fact lookups (e.g., "What year was the framework released?"), yet the coordinator routes every query through the full search → analyze → synthesize → report pipeline — averaging 60s and ~5× the token cost of a direct search. What design best addresses this?
o: Cache full-pipeline results so repeated simple queries return faster

Have the coordinator assess each query's complexity and dynamically invoke only the subagents required — e.g., a single search subagent for a simple lookup — reserving the full pipeline for complex topics
Keep running the full pipeline but cut each subagent's token budget on simple queries
Permanently remove the analyze and report subagents so every query runs faster
bank.w: A coordinator should match effort to query complexity, invoking only the subagents needed.  A caching helps repeats, not first-time simple queries, and adds invalidation complexity; C still runs the whole pipeline; D removing stages breaks complex queries.

bank.q: You run the system on "the global shift to renewable energy." Every subagent succeeds and the final report is coherent — but it covers only solar power, omitting wind, hydro, and geothermal. The coordinator's log shows it decomposed the topic into "residential solar," "utility-scale solar," and "solar manufacturing." What is the most likely root cause?
o: The coordinator's task decomposition was too narrow — its subtopic assignments (all solar) don't span the full topic, so whole areas were never researched
The search subagent's queries weren't comprehensive enough and need broader keywords
The synthesize subagent dropped the non-solar findings during aggregation
The document-analysis subagent over-filtered non-solar sources as irrelevant
bank.w: The log shows the decomposition itself was too narrow (all solar); the subagents executed their assignments correctly.  B/C/D all blame downstream agents that worked as instructed — the root cause is upstream decomposition.

bank.q: The coordinator needs to run three independent searches concurrently to cut latency. How does it spawn them in parallel?
o: Set `tool_choice: "any"` so the model issues all three searches at once
Call `fork_session` three times to create three branches
Lower each search subagent's timeout so all three return quickly
Emit multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response — calls in one response run in parallel, whereas one call per turn runs sequentially
bank.w: Parallel subagents come from emitting multiple Task calls in one response; one-per-turn is serial.  A `tool_choice: "any"` only forces a tool call; B `fork_session` is for divergent branches, not parallel search; C timeouts don't create concurrency.

bank.q: Your coordinator is supposed to delegate to subagents but never does — it attempts every task itself. A config review shows its `allowedTools` list omits "Task". What is the fix and why?
o: Add explicit few-shot examples in the system prompt showing the coordinator delegating
Increase the coordinator's subagent count in its AgentDefinition
Add "Task" to the coordinator's `allowedTools`: the Task tool is the mechanism for spawning subagents and must be permitted for delegation to occur
Rewrite the coordinator prompt with step-by-step procedural delegation instructions
bank.w: The Task tool spawns subagents and must be in `allowedTools`.  A/D are prompt tweaks that can't grant a missing capability; B more subagents in the definition is useless if the tool to invoke them is disallowed.

bank.q: The synthesize subagent produces a generic, high-level write-up that never references the specific sources and figures the search and analyze subagents found earlier in the coordinator's conversation. Those subagents returned correct, detailed results. What is the most likely cause and fix?
o: Subagents don't automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history; the coordinator must include the prior findings explicitly in the synthesize subagent's prompt
The synthesize subagent's context window is too small to hold the findings
The coordinator should lower the synthesize subagent's temperature to keep it grounded
The synthesize subagent needs a higher `max_tokens` to include the details
bank.w: Subagents don't inherit the coordinator's history — findings must be passed in the prompt.  B capacity isn't the issue (the data was never provided); C temperature is irrelevant to missing context; D more output budget doesn't supply absent input.

bank.q: Audit logs show that in 9% of refund cases the agent calls `process_refund` without first calling `lookup_order`, so it occasionally refunds ineligible orders (already refunded, or outside the return window). Order eligibility is a hard business rule. What most reliably enforces "verify the order before refunding"?
o: Strengthen the system prompt to state that `lookup_order` must always precede `process_refund`
Add a programmatic prerequisite gate that rejects any `process_refund` call unless a successful `lookup_order` result for that order is present in the session state
Add few-shot examples showing the agent calling `lookup_order` before `process_refund`
Add a routing classifier that enables `process_refund` only for refund-type requests
bank.w: A prerequisite gate gives a deterministic guarantee for a hard business rule.  A/C are probabilistic prompting — the non-zero failure rate is exactly the 9%; D controls which tools are available, not the order they run in.

bank.q: A single customer message contains three distinct issues (a billing error, a damaged item, and an address change). The agent resolves only the first and ends the turn. What workflow design best handles this?
o: Ask the customer to resubmit one issue per message
Escalate to a human because three simultaneous issues exceed the agent's scope
Handle exactly one issue per conversation turn across several turns
Decompose the multi-concern request into distinct items, investigate each (in parallel where possible) using shared context, then synthesize one unified resolution
bank.w: Decompose the multi-concern request, handle each with shared context, then synthesize one resolution.  A offloads to the customer; B over-escalates a handleable case; C is slow and disjointed.

bank.q: When the agent escalates a complex billing dispute via `escalate_to_human`, the human agent — who has no access to the chat transcript — receives only the line "Escalating billing issue." Handle time is high because they must re-gather everything. What should the handoff include?
o: The complete raw conversation transcript, copied verbatim
A short apology message the human can forward to the customer
A structured handoff summary: the customer ID, the root-cause analysis, the disputed amount, and a recommended action
The agent's confidence score that escalation was the right call
bank.w: A structured handoff (ID, root cause, amount, recommended action) lets a human without the transcript act immediately.  A a raw transcript dump is unusable and they can't access it anyway; B/D don't transfer the case facts.

bank.q: Policy requires human approval for any refund over $500, but the agent occasionally processes larger refunds when its prompt-based self-check fails. What provides a guaranteed block?
o: A tool-call interception hook that blocks `process_refund` calls above $500 and redirects them to the human-escalation workflow
A stronger, more explicit system-prompt instruction restating the $500 limit
Few-shot examples demonstrating refunds over $500 being escalated
A programmatic check inside `process_refund` that asks the model to confirm the amount is allowed
bank.w: A tool-call interception hook deterministically blocks the over-limit action.  B/C are probabilistic prompting; D still routes the decision through the fallible model instead of enforcing it.

bank.q: Three MCP tools return dates differently — `get_customer` uses ISO 8601, `lookup_order` uses Unix epoch seconds, and a legacy status tool returns numeric codes. The agent misreads them ~15% of the time when reasoning about timelines. You need every result normalized to one format before the model reasons over it, every time. What's the most reliable mechanism?
o: A system-prompt section documenting each tool's format and asking the model to convert them
A PostToolUse hook that transforms each tool's output into a single normalized date format before the model processes it
Few-shot examples showing correct interpretation of each format
A note in CLAUDE.md describing the three date formats
bank.w: A PostToolUse hook normalizes formats deterministically before the model reasons over them.  A/C/D are all prompt-based and probabilistic — the source of the 15% misreads.

bank.q: You need a code review that runs the same predictable steps on every PR: a lint check, then a security scan, then a test-coverage check. Which decomposition strategy fits?
o: Dynamic adaptive decomposition that generates the steps based on what each pass discovers
A single prompt instructing the agent to do all three checks at once
Three parallel subagents with no coordinator to merge findings
A fixed sequential pipeline (prompt chaining) — the steps are predictable and identical each run, so chain them in a defined order
bank.w: Predictable, identical steps suit a fixed prompt-chaining pipeline.  A dynamic decomposition is for open-ended work; B doing all at once dilutes attention; C uncoordinated parallel passes can't merge.

bank.q: You ask the agent to "find and fix the performance bottlenecks in this 200-file service." The bottlenecks aren't known in advance, and fixing one may reveal others. Which task-decomposition strategy fits best?
o: A fixed pipeline that optimizes each file once, in directory order
A single prompt instructing the agent to "fix all performance issues now"
A dynamic, adaptive plan: profile to locate hotspots, fix the highest-impact one, then re-profile and let the next steps adapt to what changed
Parallel subagents, one per file, each optimizing independently with no coordination
bank.w: Unknown, interacting bottlenecks call for adaptive decomposition that re-plans as it learns.  A fixed order ignores impact and interactions; B one shot won't surface hidden hotspots; D uncoordinated per-file work misses cross-file effects.

bank.q: You resume a named codebase-analysis session with `--resume` the next morning, but teammates modified several files overnight. The agent answers from its now-stale earlier analysis. What's the best practice?
o: Inform the resumed session which specific files changed so it re-analyzes those; if most prior context is now invalid, start fresh with an injected summary instead of resuming on stale tool results
Always start completely fresh and never use `--resume`
Resume and trust the prior analysis — overnight file changes rarely affect results
Use `fork_session` to branch from the stale analysis and continue there
bank.w: Tell the resumed session which files changed for targeted re-analysis; if context is largely stale, start fresh with a summary.  B is absolutist and wasteful; C trusts stale state; D forking keeps the stale baseline.

bank.q: From a shared baseline analysis of a codebase, you want to compare two different refactoring approaches side by side — without one polluting the other's context — then pick the better result. Which mechanism fits?
o: Use `--resume` to reopen the same session twice and try both approaches in it
Use `fork_session` to create two independent branches from the shared baseline analysis, explore each approach separately, then compare
Lower the temperature and ask the agent to weigh both approaches in one response
Start two completely unrelated sessions with no shared baseline
bank.w: `fork_session` creates independent branches from a shared baseline — ideal for comparing approaches without cross-contamination.  A reusing one session lets the branches pollute each other; C is one context, not a true side-by-side; D loses the shared baseline.

bank.q: A research agent has two tools, `analyze_content` and `analyze_document`, with near-identical descriptions. It routes web-search results to the wrong one in about 20% of cases. What's the most effective first step?
o: Add 5–8 few-shot examples in the system prompt showing the correct routing
Add a routing layer that inspects the input and pre-selects the tool before each turn
Rename and rewrite the descriptions to eliminate the functional overlap (e.g., `extract_web_results` with a clearly web-specific description) so each tool's purpose is distinct
Force `tool_choice` to `analyze_document` whenever a document is present
bank.w: Overlapping descriptions cause misrouting; renaming/differentiating them fixes the root cause at low effort.  A adds token overhead without resolving the ambiguity; B over-engineers and bypasses the model's language understanding; D forcing a tool ignores cases where the other is correct.

bank.q: Your tool descriptions are thorough, yet the agent still over-calls `get_customer` even for order-only questions. You notice the system prompt repeats "always confirm the customer first." What should you check?
o: The system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions that create unintended tool associations and can override well-written descriptions
Whether `get_customer`'s description is too long and should be shortened to one line
Whether the two tools should be merged into a single `lookup_entity` tool
Whether `tool_choice` should be set to "any" to force a choice
bank.w: Keyword-sensitive system-prompt wording can create unintended tool associations that override good descriptions — inspect the prompt.  B shortening descriptions usually worsens selection; C/D are heavier changes that don't address the actual cause.

bank.q: An agent has two MCP tools, `search_code` and `lookup_ticket`, each with a one-line description ("Searches the codebase" / "Looks things up"). It routes ticket queries like "what's the status of PROJ-481?" to `search_code` ~25% of the time. What's the most effective first step?
o: Add a routing layer that detects ticket-ID patterns and pre-selects the tool
Merge the two tools into one lookup tool that inspects the input
Force `tool_choice` to `lookup_ticket` whenever the message contains a hyphenated ID
Expand each tool's description to specify the inputs it accepts, example queries, edge cases, and when to use it versus the similar tool
bank.w: Tool descriptions are the primary selection mechanism; enriching them with inputs, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries is the low-effort, high-leverage first step.  A is over-engineered; B merging discards a useful distinction; C a brittle pattern rule bypasses the model.

bank.q: Your agent has one broad `manage_account` tool that updates addresses, changes plans, or closes accounts depending on a free-form action argument. The agent frequently picks the wrong action and mis-edits accounts. What design most improves reliability?
o: Add "choose the action carefully" to the tool's description
Split `manage_account` into purpose-specific tools (`update_address`, `change_plan`, `close_account`) with defined input/output contracts
Keep one tool but constrain the action argument to an enum of allowed values
Force `tool_choice` to `manage_account` so it is always used
bank.w: Splitting a broad multi-purpose tool into purpose-specific tools with clear contracts gives the model clearer selection signals and enables per-action permissions.  A is vague; C an enum helps but still routes everything through one risky tool; D forcing the tool doesn't fix wrong-action selection.

bank.q: `lookup_order` returns no rows for a valid query because the customer genuinely has no orders, but the tool returns the same error shape as a timeout. The agent retries pointlessly, then tells the customer something went wrong. What's the correct design?
o: Distinguish a valid empty result (successful query, no matches) from an access failure (e.g., a timeout needing a retry decision), so the agent reports "no orders found" instead of retrying
Mark all empty results as transient errors with `isRetryable: true`
Return the customer's most recent historical order when the current query is empty
Treat an empty result as a permission error and escalate to a human
bank.w: A valid empty result must be distinguished from an access failure so the agent responds correctly instead of retrying.  B causes the pointless retries; C returns wrong data; D mislabels a normal outcome as a permission problem.

bank.q: A search subagent hits an intermittent timeout mid-task. How should error handling be structured for reliable recovery?
o: Immediately propagate every error to the coordinator without local retries
Catch the timeout and return an empty result marked as successful
Throw the timeout to a top-level handler that aborts the entire research run
Retry transient failures locally inside the subagent, and propagate to the coordinator only errors it cannot resolve — including what was attempted and any partial results
bank.w: Recover transient errors locally; propagate only the unresolvable ones, with partial results and what was attempted.  A floods the coordinator; B suppresses failure as success (anti-pattern); C aborts unnecessarily.

bank.q: Your MCP tools return every failure as `{"error": "failed"}`. The agent retries policy violations (which can never succeed), gives up immediately on timeouts, and tells customers "something went wrong" for normal empty results. What's the most effective redesign?
o: Wrap every tool call in a global retry-three-times policy
Log all errors server-side and have the agent apologize generically
Return structured errors with an `errorCategory` (transient / validation / business / permission) and an `isRetryable` boolean, plus a human-readable message
Map every failure to a transient error so the agent retries consistently
bank.w: Structured errors with a category + `isRetryable` let the agent retry only what's retryable and explain business violations appropriately.  A blind global retries waste calls on non-retryable failures; B loses the recovery signal; D mislabeling everything transient guarantees wasted retries.

bank.q: In your pipeline, `extract_metadata` must always run before any enrichment tools. How do you guarantee the metadata tool is called first?
o: Set `tool_choice: "auto"` and order the tool definitions so `extract_metadata` is listed first
Use forced tool selection (`tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}`) on the first turn, then handle enrichment in follow-up turns
Set `tool_choice: "any"` so the model is required to call some tool first
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to call `extract_metadata` before anything else
bank.w: Forced tool selection guarantees `extract_metadata` runs first; later steps proceed in follow-up turns.  A ordering definitions doesn't guarantee order; C "any" doesn't pin which tool; D prompt instructions are probabilistic.

bank.q: A document-analysis subagent has a generic `fetch_url` tool and sometimes pulls arbitrary, irrelevant web pages. What's the best constraint?
o: Replace `fetch_url` with a constrained `load_document` tool that validates document URLs, limiting the subagent to appropriate inputs
Give every subagent `fetch_url` so behavior is consistent across roles
Remove all tools from the subagent and have the coordinator fetch for it
Keep `fetch_url` but add a system-prompt rule listing banned domains
bank.w: Replacing a generic tool with a constrained, validating alternative scopes the subagent to appropriate inputs.  B spreads the problem; C strips needed capability; D a prompt denylist is fragile versus a validating contract.

bank.q: Each subagent (search, analyze, synthesize, report) is given the full set of 16 tools "for flexibility." Tool-selection accuracy is poor — the synthesize subagent sometimes launches web searches and the search subagent tries to write reports. What's the best fix?
o: Keep all 16 tools available to every subagent but add detailed few-shot examples for each role
Increase each subagent's reasoning budget so it can deliberate over all 16 tools
Merge the four subagents into one agent that holds all 16 tools
Scope each subagent to only the tools its role needs, granting at most a narrow cross-role tool for a specific high-frequency need
bank.w: Too many tools (16 vs ~4–5) and tools outside a role's specialization degrade selection; scope each subagent to its role with at most a narrow cross-role tool.  A doesn't reduce decision complexity; B capacity isn't the issue; C merging makes the overload worse.

bank.q: Your extraction step sometimes returns a chatty natural-language answer instead of calling an extraction tool, which breaks the downstream parser. You must guarantee the model calls a tool every time, though which extraction tool depends on the document. Which setting fits?
o: `tool_choice: "auto"` — let the model decide whether to call a tool
`tool_choice: "any"` — the model must call a tool but may choose which
Force one specific tool with `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}` regardless of document type
Add "always use a tool, never reply in prose" to the system prompt
bank.w: `tool_choice: "any"` forces a tool call (guaranteeing structured output) while letting the model choose the right schema.  A may return prose; C forcing one schema mishandles other document types; D prompt instructions don't guarantee a tool call.

bank.q: Your agent burns many tool calls exploring which Jira issues exist before it can act. You want to give it up-front visibility into available issues. Which MCP mechanism fits best?
o: Add several more granular search tools so exploration is faster
Paste the full issue list into the system prompt on every request
Expose the issue summaries as an MCP resource (a content catalog) so the agent has visibility into available data without exploratory tool calls
Add a `list_all_issues` tool the agent must call at the start of every turn
bank.w: MCP resources expose content catalogs so the agent sees available data without exploratory calls.  A more tools doesn't reduce exploration; B re-pasting wastes context each request; D a mandatory per-turn call is wasteful and rigid.

bank.q: Your team needs standard Jira integration. Building a custom MCP server would take weeks. What's the appropriate choice?
o: Use an existing community MCP server for the standard Jira integration, reserving custom servers for genuinely team-specific workflows
Build a custom MCP server for full control, regardless of the time cost
Skip MCP and have developers paste Jira data into the conversation manually
Use the built-in Grep tool to search the Jira web UI's HTML
bank.w: Prefer an existing community server for standard integrations; reserve custom builds for team-specific needs.  B ignores cost for no added value; C abandons automation; D misuses Grep (it searches local file contents, not a web UI).

bank.q: You're testing a brand-new, unstable MCP server on your own machine and don't want it to affect teammates or land in the repo. Separately, the team's stable GitHub MCP server should be shared with everyone via the repo, authenticated by a token that must not be committed. How do you configure each?
o: Both servers in project-scoped `.mcp.json` so everything lives in one place
Both servers in `~/.claude.json` so each developer controls their own setup
The shared server in `.mcp.json` with the token hard-coded; the experimental one in the project CLAUDE.md
The experimental server in your user-scoped `~/.claude.json`; the shared GitHub server in project-scoped `.mcp.json` with the token via env-var expansion (`${GITHUB_TOKEN}`)
bank.w: Personal/experimental servers belong in user-scoped `~/.claude.json`; shared team servers in project-scoped `.mcp.json`, with secrets via env-var expansion so nothing is committed.  A would share the experimental server; B wouldn't share the team server; C commits the secret and misuses CLAUDE.md (which doesn't configure servers).

bank.q: You need to (1) find every file whose name matches `**/*.test.tsx`, and separately (2) find all callers of a function named `processPayment`. Which built-in tools fit, respectively?
o: Grep for both tasks
Glob for the filename-pattern search; Grep for the function-content search
Glob for both tasks
Bash `ls` for the first; Read on each file for the second
bank.w: Glob matches file paths by name/extension; Grep searches file contents (e.g., callers of a function).  A/C use the wrong tool for one half; D is slower and less reliable than the purpose-built tools.

bank.q: An Edit operation fails because the target text appears in several places in the file (a non-unique match). What's the reliable fallback?
o: Retry the same Edit repeatedly until it succeeds
Use Grep to locate and replace the text in place
Use Read to load the full file contents, then Write the modified file — the Read+Write fallback handles cases where Edit can't find a unique anchor
Delete the file with Bash and recreate it from memory with Write
bank.w: When Edit can't find a unique anchor, the Read+Write fallback reliably applies the change.  A repeating the same Edit fails identically; B Grep searches, it doesn't edit; D recreating from memory risks data loss/fabrication.

bank.q: You must understand how authentication flows through an unfamiliar 500-file codebase. What's the most effective way to use the built-in tools?
o: Read every file in the repository once, in order, to build complete understanding
Use Glob to list all files, then Read them alphabetically
Have the agent describe a typical authentication flow from general knowledge
Use Grep to find the entry points (e.g., the auth middleware), then Read to follow the imports and trace the flow, expanding only as needed
bank.w: Build understanding incrementally — Grep to entry points, then Read to follow imports — rather than reading everything upfront.  A/B read-all strategies waste context and time; C general knowledge isn't grounded in this codebase.

bank.q: Your root CLAUDE.md has grown huge with standards for many packages and is unwieldy. Each package's maintainers want only their relevant standards loaded. What's the cleanest approach?
o: Keep one large root CLAUDE.md and rely on Claude to find the relevant section per package
Move all standards into the user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
Delete any standards that don't apply to every package
Use the `@import` syntax to reference external standards files, including only the relevant ones in each package's CLAUDE.md
bank.w: `@import` keeps CLAUDE.md modular — each package pulls in only the standards files it needs.  A relies on inference over a bloated file; B user-level config isn't shared via version control; C discards legitimately package-specific standards.

bank.q: Claude Code behaves inconsistently across sessions and you suspect the wrong CLAUDE.md/memory files are loading. How do you diagnose which are actually active?
o: Delete all CLAUDE.md files and rebuild them from scratch
Use the `/memory` command to verify which memory files are currently loaded
Restart the session repeatedly until behavior stabilizes
Move everything to a single root CLAUDE.md and assume that one loads
bank.w: `/memory` shows which memory/config files are loaded — the direct diagnostic.  A (delete/rebuild) is destructive guesswork; C (restart) is trial-and-error; D assumes rather than verifies.

bank.q: Your coding standards are documented and working on your machine, but a contractor who just cloned the repo reports that Claude Code ignores them entirely. You realize you put the standards in your own `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Why does the contractor not get them, and what's the fix?
o: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is user-level (not version-controlled), so it never reaches teammates; move the standards to the project-level root CLAUDE.md (or `.claude/`) so they're shared
The contractor's Claude Code version is out of date and needs upgrading
The contractor must run `/memory` to manually load your `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
Directory-level CLAUDE.md files override user-level ones, so the standards must be duplicated into every subdirectory
bank.w: Instructions in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` are user-scoped and never travel with the repo; move them to project-level config.  B/C misattribute the cause; D is false — directory-level files don't "override" user-level this way and don't require duplication.

bank.q: You build a `/security-review` slash command encoding your team's checklist. Every developer should get it automatically when they clone or pull the repo. Where should the command file live?
o: In `~/.claude/commands/` in each developer's home directory
In `.claude/commands/` in the project repository
In the project root CLAUDE.md under a "Commands" heading
In a `.claude/config.json` file with a commands array
bank.w: Project-scoped commands live in `.claude/commands/` and are shared via version control.  A is personal/user scope; C CLAUDE.md holds context, not command definitions; D `.claude/config.json` is a non-existent mechanism.

bank.q: Your `/audit-dependencies` skill emits hundreds of lines of dependency-tree output that swamp the main conversation and push out the context you need for the actual fix. Which frontmatter setting best addresses this?
o: `allowed-tools` — restrict which tools the skill can use
`argument-hint` — prompt for parameters at invocation
`context: fork` — run the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so its verbose output doesn't pollute the main conversation
Move the skill to `~/.claude/skills/` so it's personal to you

Whether raising the model's confidence threshold pushes overall accuracy higher
